story.introAr: An unknown force from outside is attacking how we think, with rumours, fake clips and fake accounts. Ride the power board and defend our national identity with Cyber!
story.winAr: Awareness wins! Thanks to you our identity stays strong, and no rumour or fake clip fools our minds.
story.simulatedNoteAr: Everything in the game is pretend: the names, accounts, news, clips and rials are not real.

sources: UNICEF, guidance for children and families on staying safe online, and Cyberbullying: What is it and how to stop it
UNESCO, Media and Information Literacy curriculum: Think Critically, Click Wisely (sources, rumours and false information)
ITU, Guidelines on Child Online Protection (privacy, contact with strangers, reporting)
Common Sense Media, Digital Citizenship curriculum (digital footprint, privacy, news and media literacy)

variants.sceneAr: An account called “Breaking News 24” has a post with no source and thousands of likes:

message.textAr: Breaking! Schools are off for a whole week from tomorrow! 🔥

options.labelAr: I look for it on the school's or ministry's official account
I cheer and tell my friends: no school!
Thousands of likes are enough. It's true

variants.explainAr: Likes don't make a thing true. The official body itself announces a holiday. If it's real, you'll find it there.

variants.sceneAr: Hours before the national team's match, an account you don't know posts:

message.textAr: Shock! Tonight's match is off and the team's star is banned! Details later…

options.labelAr: It's all over the feed, so it must be true
I open the football association's official account
I tell Dad and my brothers the match is off

variants.explainAr: “Details later” with no source is a sign of a rumour. Real news is on the official account before any unknown one.

variants.sceneAr: Your family is about to drive to Salalah for khareef. Your sister believes this post:

message.textAr: Salalah road closed to cars from today! Don't travel!

variants.promptAr: What do you tell your sister?

options.labelAr: We tell Dad to cancel the trip now
Many people shared it, so it must be true
First we check the police's official account

variants.explainAr: The body in charge of roads announces this on its official account. A post with no source is no reason to change plans.

variants.sceneAr: This message lands in the family group, marked “Forwarded many times”:

message.textAr: Warning! A famous juice in the shops is poisonous. Send to all you love before it's deleted!

options.labelAr: I send it at once to my class group and friends
I don't send it. I ask for a source and check official accounts
I send it just in case. It can't hurt if it's wrong

variants.explainAr: “Share before it's deleted” is rumour talk. A wrong message does harm: it scares people and wrongs others.

variants.sceneAr: In the class group a classmate sends this, and everyone starts forwarding it:

message.textAr: They say tomorrow's test leaked and is cancelled! Send to every class, quick 🙏

options.labelAr: I don't forward it. I wait for the teacher or school platform
Only to my brother's class. It may be true
I send it to every group, as he asked

variants.explainAr: “They say” is not a source. If classmates believed it, they'd stop studying over a message nobody checked.

variants.sceneAr: A few days before Eid you get this message from your cousin:

message.textAr: A free Eid gift for every child from a big company! Send this to 20 people to get yours 🎁

options.labelAr: I send it to a few friends. I've nothing to lose
I send it to 20 people to get the Eid gift
I don't send it, and I tell Said nobody has checked it

variants.explainAr: Nobody gives out gifts by counting forwards. These messages only want to spread, and stop when we don't send them.

variants.sceneAr: You get a clip of a famous news presenter saying odd things. His lips don't quite match his voice:

message.textAr: “New decision: there will be school on Fridays too!”

options.labelAr: I believe it. I saw and heard it myself
I doubt it and check the channel's official account
I send it to friends for a laugh, even if it's fake

variants.explainAr: AI can copy faces and voices. If the clip is not on the official account, don't believe it and don't share it.

variants.sceneAr: A viral photo: your favourite national team player holds a sign insulting his fans. His hand has six fingers!

options.labelAr: I think it's fake and check his verified account
I post it and ask: “Is this true?”
A photo is proof. I won't cheer for him again

variants.explainAr: Small mistakes like extra fingers give made-up photos away. Posting it, even with a question, helps it spread.

variants.sceneAr: A short clip from an interview with a well-known person is cut in the middle. He seems to mock young people.

options.labelAr: I send it to the group with a joke
He said it himself. No need to check
I look for the full interview at its source before I judge

variants.explainAr: A sentence cut from its place changes meaning. The full interview at its source shows what was really said.

variants.sceneAr: Scrolling the clip app “Lamha”, you see a clip with words and acts that don't fit our upbringing.

options.labelAr: I skip it, tap “Not interested”, and tell Mum
I watch it all. Being curious can't hurt
I send it to my friend: did you see this?

variants.explainAr: The app shows you more of what you watch to the end. Skipping and “Not interested” teach it what suits you.

variants.sceneAr: In the majlis on Eid day, your cousin shows you a “famous” clip whose maker mocks respecting parents.

options.labelAr: I ask him to send it so I can show my friends
I say it's not for us. We report it and tell a grown-up
We watch it again together. It's only a joke

variants.explainAr: Fame doesn't make a clip right. Respecting parents is one of our values, and reporting it means fewer people see it.

variants.sceneAr: After a football clip, the app starts suggesting an account that pushes a way of life against our family's values.

options.labelAr: I watch a few to see what it's about
I share them in the friends' group to comment
I choose “Don't suggest this account” and talk to Dad

variants.explainAr: What you watch today is what the app suggests tomorrow. Talking with your parents helps you understand what you saw.

variants.sceneAr: A new trend: the “Jump Challenge”. Your friends jump off a high wall and film it, and say: “Your turn!”

options.labelAr: I say no, warn them, and tell my teacher or Dad
I jump just once to get views
I don't jump, but I film them and post it

variants.explainAr: Courage is saying “no” in front of friends. Filming and posting pushes others to copy what can hurt them.

variants.sceneAr: A trend going round: filming a humiliating prank on old people. Your friend wants to try it on the old sweet seller.

options.labelAr: I only hold the phone and film while he does it
I refuse, say respecting elders is our way, and tell my family
We try it once. Everyone does it and people laugh

variants.explainAr: A quick laugh isn't worth humiliating a person. Respecting elders is our way. Whoever films an insult shares in it.

variants.sceneAr: At the National Day parade a trend spreads: leaning out of a moving car to film. Your cousin wants you both to try.

options.labelAr: I lean out a little. The car is slow
I stay seated and film him doing it to post it
I say no, warn him, and tell Dad if he insists

variants.explainAr: We celebrate our country safe and sound. A trend that endangers you isn't worth copying or filming.

variants.sceneAr: An unknown account posts a picture mocking the dishdasha and massar, writing: “Who'll defend it? Reply to me!”

options.labelAr: I don't reply. I report the account and block it
I reply with a worse insult to teach him
I repost it so everyone sees it and attacks him

variants.explainAr: He wants replies because each reply spreads his post further. Reporting and blocking deny him that.

variants.sceneAr: Under a clip about Omani halwa and coffee, a new account mocks our accent and customs. Your brother is very angry.
variants.promptAr: What do you tell your brother?

options.labelAr: Mock his accent and customs back
Screenshot and post his comments to anger everyone
Don't argue: report and block him. Let's be proud calmly

variants.explainAr: The account was made to provoke. Mocking back makes us look bad, and calm pride makes his plan fail.

variants.sceneAr: During National Day a post mocks our flag and our celebration, with hundreds of angry comments under it.

options.labelAr: I share it on my account: “Look what he says!”
I report and block it, and post a lovely photo of our day
I add an angry comment like the others

variants.explainAr: Hundreds of angry comments carried the post further. The best reply is to show the world what we're proud of.

variants.sceneAr: First day of school. You took a photo outside your house in school uniform. The house number and school badge show.

options.labelAr: I send it to the family group only, or hide the number and badge
I post it now for all and add my home location
I post it for all as is. Who'd notice the number?

variants.explainAr: The house number and school badge tell a stranger where you live and study. Such a photo belongs with family.

variants.sceneAr: Your family is in Salalah for a whole week, and the house is empty. You took a great photo at the waterfall.
variants.promptAr: When and how do you post it?

options.labelAr: Now, with the location and “A whole week in Salalah!”
After we come back, with no location tag
Now, no location, but I write our house is empty all week

variants.explainAr: Posting live tells everyone where you are and that the house is empty. The photo is just as nice after you return.

variants.sceneAr: You're at the stadium with your brother for the match, and want to start a live video everyone on the app can see.

options.labelAr: I go live for all and say our seat number so friends find us
I go live for everyone with live location on
I film, then send clips after the match to family and friends

variants.explainAr: Going live for everyone shows any stranger where you are right now. Sharing clips later with people you know is safer.

variants.sceneAr: A quiz going round your friends: “Which hero are you?”. Before the result it asks:

message.textAr: Type your full name, birthday, school name and your dad's phone number.

options.labelAr: I close the quiz. Fun doesn't need these details
I type it all to get my result like my friends
I type only my name and school. They're no secret

variants.explainAr: Your name, school and birthday together tell strangers who you are. A quiz that asks for them just collects data.

variants.sceneAr: A link in the class group: “Find out your future job!”. The first questions are fun, then this appears:

message.textAr: For your result: your mum's full name, your home address and a clear photo of your face.

options.labelAr: I send only the photo and leave the rest empty
I stop here and warn my classmates in the group
I go on. I've answered most of it and won't quit now

variants.explainAr: The fun first questions are bait. Your mum's name, your address and your photo belong to your whole family.

variants.sceneAr: An Eid “Wheel of Luck” game promises a gift. First it wants your details and those of three friends.

options.labelAr: I type my details and my friends' so we all win
I type only my friends' details and keep mine
I type no one's details, not even mine, and close the game

variants.explainAr: Your friends' details are a trust, not yours to give away. A real gift isn't bought with people's names and numbers.

variants.sceneAr: With your parents' OK, you made an account on the app “Nabd”. The app asks: who can see your photos?

options.labelAr: “Private”: only people I know and approve see them
“Public”: so I get more followers fast
“Private”, but I accept everyone who asks to follow

variants.explainAr: A private account works only if you accept people you truly know. Accepting everyone makes it public again.

variants.sceneAr: Your account is private. Today 30 unknown accounts asked to follow you, and your friend has a thousand followers.

options.labelAr: I accept them all. Lots of followers is nice
I make my account public to beat my friend
I decline strangers and keep my account private

variants.explainAr: A stranger who follows you sees your photos and family news. Privacy is worth more than any follower count.

variants.sceneAr: You sit with your big sister to check your account settings. You find it is “Public” and anyone can message you.

options.labelAr: We leave it public. Nothing has happened yet
We make it private, friends-only messages, and remove strangers
We make it private but keep the stranger followers

variants.explainAr: Settings get changed and forgotten, so check them with someone older. Strangers on your list see all you post.

variants.sceneAr: In the game “Valley Heroes” a stranger has praised you for days. Today he writes:

message.textAr: You're the best! Let's talk on the app “Hamsa”. Free gems for you there 💎

options.labelAr: I say no, stop the chat and tell Mum or Dad
I move to the other app to get the gems
I stay, keep chatting and tell no one

variants.explainAr: A stranger who pulls you into a private chat wants you away from your family's eyes. Free gifts are bait.

variants.sceneAr: A player on your game team says he's your age. After a week of playing together he writes:

message.textAr: Send me your photo so I see what my friend looks like! Then I'll send mine.

options.labelAr: I send just one photo. He's my friend in the game
I say sorry, and hide it from my family to keep playing
I send nothing, block him, and tell my parents

variants.explainAr: You can't know who is behind the screen, whatever he says. Telling your parents is what really protects you.

variants.sceneAr: Someone you met in a game sent you a gift there, then wrote:

message.textAr: This gift is our secret 🤫 Don't tell your family, and I'll send more.

options.labelAr: I don't reply, but I keep it secret
I tell my parents at once and stop talking to him
I accept his rule and ask for another gift

variants.explainAr: Whoever asks you to hide things from your family knows they'd protect you. It's the clearest sign to stop and tell.

variants.sceneAr: In the class group someone posts a funny edited photo of your classmate Hamad, and laughing faces pour in.

options.labelAr: I screenshot the chat, support Hamad, and tell the teacher
I send a laughing face like everyone. It's a joke
I insult the one who posted it, in front of all

variants.explainAr: What makes all laugh and hurts one is bullying, not a joke. Saved proof and telling a grown-up stop it.

variants.sceneAr: A new girl joined the class group, and some classmates began to mock the way she talks in voice notes.

options.labelAr: I mock them back harder so they feel it too
I welcome her, save the messages, and tell the teacher or Mum
I laugh along so they don't mock me too

variants.explainAr: One word of welcome can change your classmate's day. Mocking back makes it worse, but grown-ups can stop it.

variants.sceneAr: Your classmate Saif missed a penalty at school. Tonight the group is full of stickers mocking him. He's silent.

options.labelAr: I send one light sticker. He won't mind
I write: “You're worse and dumber than him!”
I send him a kind word, save the chat, and tell the coach

variants.explainAr: Silence doesn't mean he's fine. Your support helps, and telling the coach stops the mocking without a new fight.

variants.sceneAr: A new, unverified account with a famous player's name writes:

message.textAr: You won my shirt! Send your full name, address and your dad's number.

options.labelAr: I check his verified account. I send nothing
I send the details fast
It's his name. I follow and tell friends

variants.explainAr: A name and photo are copied in seconds. The old verified account is the real one. Stars don't ask for your details by message.

variants.sceneAr: A relative shares an account named after a known charity:

message.textAr: Donate now to our new number, and send a photo of your dad's card.

variants.promptAr: What do you tell your family?

options.labelAr: It has the charity's logo, so we share it
We check the charity's verified account first
We send a little now. Good can't wait

variants.explainAr: Scammers use people's love of doing good. Give through the charity's official channels, and nobody asks for a photo of a card.

variants.sceneAr: A new account with your school's name and logo posts:

message.textAr: Big contest! Send your details and a 2 rial fee to this account's owner.

options.labelAr: I send my details and the fee
I follow it and repost it to my class
I ask the teacher or check the school's real account

variants.explainAr: The school announces contests through its own channels and teachers. A new account asking for money and details deserves doubt.

variants.sceneAr: Under a normal local news post: dozens of angry comments, all the very same sentence, from accounts with no photos.

options.labelAr: I open a few accounts: new, no followers. I don't trust them
All these people are angry, so some of it is true
I copy and post the sentence. Everyone says it

variants.explainAr: Real people don't write the exact same sentence. These are fake accounts made to make you think everyone is angry.

variants.sceneAr: An angry hashtag against a festival in your city suddenly trends. Most accounts posting in it were made this week.

options.labelAr: I join the hashtag with an angry post too
I see the accounts are new and alike, so I don't follow along
A top hashtag means the whole city is angry

variants.explainAr: Many fake accounts can push a hashtag up. Trending shows how much is posted, not how true it is or what people think.

variants.sceneAr: Your friend shows you a post attacking your country's youth and says: “Look, 5,000 comments agree! It must be true.”

options.labelAr: You're right. 5,000 people can't be wrong
Let's post what they say too, so we're not left out
Numbers aren't proof. Who are they? When were the accounts made?

variants.explainAr: Truth isn't found by counting comments. Always ask: who says it? What's the proof? Why do they repeat the same words?

variants.sceneAr: An unknown number invites you to a closed channel:

message.textAr: “The truth they hide from you” 🔒 Join now and tell no one. Places are limited!

options.labelAr: I don't join. I delete it and tell Mum or Dad
I join to learn the secrets before places run out
I join quietly and only read, no writing

variants.explainAr: “Tell no one” is a danger sign. Whoever has the truth doesn't hide it in a closed channel, and quiet reading still affects you.

variants.sceneAr: A stranger adds you to a group where you know no one. Every message is angry and urges hating your own community.

options.labelAr: I stay and watch quietly, out of curiosity
I leave the group, report it, and show my parents
I join the talk to learn why they are angry

variants.explainAr: Anger groups are built to change your thinking bit by bit. Leaving, reporting and telling your parents protects you fastest.

variants.sceneAr: A player in your game invites you to a group “for the elite only”, with “what nobody dares say about your country”.

options.labelAr: I join. Nobody refuses an “elite” invite
I pop in for a few minutes. No one will know
I turn the invite down and tell Dad what he said

variants.explainAr: Calling you “elite” is praise to pull you in. Whoever promises secrets in a closed place wants to sway you far from your family.

variants.sceneAr: A tropical storm nears the coast. An unknown man's voice note spreads in the groups:

message.textAr: “My relative there confirms: the storm will destroy everything tonight! Run!”

variants.promptAr: Where do you get your news?

options.labelAr: The weather office, civil defence and the official news
From the voice note. His relative works there
Any account that writes “Breaking” first

variants.explainAr: “My relative confirms” is no source. Official bodies track the storm and give the right instructions step by step.

variants.sceneAr: Heavy rain tonight. The groups are full of messages and voice notes that disagree about school tomorrow.
variants.promptAr: How do you find the truth?

options.labelAr: I follow unknown “Breaking” accounts. They're fastest
I wait for the ministry's notice or the school's message
I believe a voice note my classmate forwarded

variants.explainAr: The body in charge announces school closures and the school tells you. Anything else is a guess, right or wrong.

variants.sceneAr: The storm cuts the power in your area. Grandma is worried, and your brother reads her scary rumours from his phone.
variants.promptAr: What do you suggest at home?

options.labelAr: We listen to the voice notes going round for more details
We follow an unknown account: “Breaking” every minute
We open official radio and accounts, and calm Grandma

variants.explainAr: Rumours grow in times of fear and add to the worry. Official sources tell you what is really happening and what to do.
